title: The true renouncer
hook: chapter five opens with Arjuna asking Krishna to stop giving him two answers and pick one
carry: the real renouncer neither hates nor craves

segments.voice: Yesterday, karma in chapter four: brahmarpanam, brahmarpanam: giver, gift and fire are brahman, seen as one act.
screen: `KARMA.` · `THE OFFERING, THE FIRE, THE ONE WHO OFFERS.`

segments.voice: Chapter five of the Gita opens with a student losing patience. Arjuna has heard Krishna praise two things that sound like opposites. On one side, giving up action, setting it all down. On the other, action done as yoga, work done without grabbing at its fruit. Which is it? Arjuna wants one answer, stated plainly. Krishna does answer him. But the answer turns the question inside out.
screen: `TWO ANSWERS. PICK ONE.` → `ARJUNA WANTS IT PLAIN.` → `THE ANSWER TURNS THE QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Here's Krishna's reply, in paraphrase. Both roads, renouncing action and the yoga of action, lead to the highest good. But of the two, the yoga of action is the better. Then he says who the real renouncer is: the one who neither hates nor craves. Not the person who has left the house. The person who has stopped pushing and pulling inside. A verse or two later he goes further. Only children, he says, talk about the way of knowing and the way of action as two separate things. The one who sees them as one, sees. The person who knows the truth, Krishna says, thinks: I am not really the doer of anything. And he lists the day as it happens. Seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, walking, sleeping, breathing, speaking, letting go, taking hold, opening and closing the eyes. All the while, that person holds that the senses are simply moving among their objects. The commentators read this chapter differently. Shankara, the teacher of non-duality, reads true renunciation as belonging with knowledge of the Self, and action without attachment as the ground that makes that knowledge possible. Ramanuja reads the way of action as an easier road to walk, one that already carries knowledge inside it. This is why Hinduism honors two lives. A few take sannyasa, the renouncer's vow: the ochre cloth, no home, no possessions. Most stay householders, with jobs and families. Krishna's line means the householder isn't second best: whoever stops hating and craving is, in his words, always a renouncer. So karma here isn't a ledger of rewards and punishments. It's the doing nobody escapes, and who we take to be doing it.
screen: `BOTH ROADS LEAD TO THE GOOD.` · `THE RENOUNCER NEITHER HATES NOR CRAVES.` · `SEEING, HEARING, BREATHING: I DO NOTHING.` · `SHANKARA AND RAMANUJA, SAME VERSES.` · `MONK OR HOUSEHOLDER: THE SAME GOAL.` · then, large: `WHO IS DOING THE DOING?`

segments.voice: Go through Krishna's list slowly, as it happens in you right now: seeing, hearing whatever sound is in the room, touching the chair, breathing, the eyes closing. Don't try to stop any of it; just notice how much is being done without any effort from you at all. If you pray, you can rest in that noticing as your prayer; if not, simply watch the senses move among their objects.
Karma. Action, the plain fact of doing. In chapter five, the question isn't whether to act, but who we take to be acting.
Your line: the real renouncer neither hates nor craves. Tomorrow, a lotus leaf in the rain. Day nine hundred sixty-seven.
